pronunciation.approximation: 'JEE-zoh' — the first syllable is like 'jee', the second is a long, drawn 'zoh'.

pronunciation.note: Jizō is Tier 1: the macron on ō marks the long vowel of the Japanese reading. The full Sanskrit name would require retroflex and aspirated consonants not registrable in the DNS root zone.

domains.title: Earth Treasury Bodhisattva
domains.subtitle: Guardian of Children, Travelers, and the Dead
domains.lead: Jizō is the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha as known and loved in Japan: a gentle monk-like figure who refuses buddhahood until all beings, especially those in hell and the spirits of dead children, are saved. His statues stand by roadsides, cemeteries, and temples, clothed in red bibs and caps offered by grieving parents.

cards.name: Guardian of Children
cards.desc: He protects children, including mizuko, the spirits of miscarried and aborted foetuses.

cards.name: Savior of Hell-beings
cards.desc: He descends into the hell realms to rescue those tormented by their karma.

cards.name: Patron of Travelers
cards.desc: Roadside Jizō guide and protect those on journeys, both living and dead.

cards.name: Bodhisattva Vow
cards.desc: He postpones his own enlightenment until every hell is emptied.

symbols.name: Staff (khakkhara)
symbols.meaning: The ringing staff that warns small creatures underfoot and opens the gates of hell.

symbols.name: Wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi)
symbols.meaning: The gem that grants all needs and dispels the darkness of the six realms.

symbols.name: Red bib or cap
symbols.meaning: Offerings by parents for the protection of their children in the afterlife — the folk garment of Sai no Kawara.

symbols.name: Lotus seat
symbols.meaning: Purity within the muddy world of suffering.

mythology.lead: Jizō's mythology blends Indian scripture, Chinese translation, and Japanese folk belief. He is one of the most actively worshipped Buddhist figures in Japan — a bodhisattva whose statues outnumber his temples.

myths.title: The Original Vow
myths.text: The Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva Sūtra recounts that in a previous life the bodhisattva was a Brahmin maiden whose mother had slandered the Dharma. After her mother's death, the daughter made vast offerings at a temple and was transported in vision to hell, where a guardian demon told her the offerings had not yet redeemed her mother. Moved by the suffering around her, she vowed before the Buddha to save all beings in the hell realms, life after life, until not a single one remained. The sūtra frames this as an intercessory chain — the Buddha entrusts the helpless, in the long night between one buddha's passing and the next's arrival, to Kṣitigarbha's keeping. The myth's engine is refusal: heaven has no vacancy so long as hell has a single prisoner, and the bodhisattva is content to wait.

myths.title: Sai no Kawara
myths.text: On the banks of Sai no Kawara, the stony riverbed where dead children must labor, the little souls pile stones as penance for having caused their parents grief — and each night demons scatter their work. Jizō comes in the guise of a wandering monk, hides the children in the sleeves of his robe, and comforts them until their karma is spent. The red bibs and caps set on his statues are gifts intended to warm these child-spirits, since the dead feel the cold. The tale first flowers in the medieval picture scrolls and story collections, where the riverbed's naked little laborers are shown weeping over their scattered stones — and Jizō arrives with his staff ringing. It is the sentimental heart of Japanese Buddhism: hell is real, labor is endless, and yet someone keeps coming down to the riverbed, night after night, to hold the children until morning.

myths.title: The Monk Who Was Jizō
myths.text: Countless Japanese tales tell of a wandering monk who helps a traveller in distress — carrying the load, pointing the road, sharing the fire — only to vanish, leaving the traveller to realize that the monk was the roadside Jizō himself. In the most beloved version, a poor but kind farmer sweeps the snow from the statues each New Year and, having no offering, gives them his own straw hat; in the night the Jizō come in procession to thank him, and his house is blessed. The stories encode a popular theology: Jizō is not distant in a pure land but present on the road, in the rain, at the crossroads where ordinary people lose their way. In a religion of vast vows, the tales insist on small gifts — a hat, a bow, a swept stone.

myths.title: The Thirteen Gifts of the Memorial
myths.text: Japanese esoteric Buddhism folded Kṣitigarbha into its map of the afterlife. In the rites of the Thirteen Buddhas, each of the memorial services after a death — the seventh day, the forty-ninth, the hundredth, the anniversaries — is entrusted to a different bodhisattva or buddha. Jizō's own watch falls on the thirty-fifth day, when the soul has crossed the first judgment and most needs a guide; the rites of his day kept his name in the villages, and the summer Jizō-bon observances with their lanterns still light the roads for the returning dead. The assignment is telling: the church gave the freshly dead, still close to the living, to the one bodhisattva who specializes in the helpless. Between the funeral and the first anniversary, salvation is less a doctrine than a relay, and Jizō runs the longest leg of it.

lore.syncretism: Kṣitigarbha entered China from India and absorbed functions of local earth gods and tomb guardians. In Japan he merged with the kami of roads and boundaries (Sae no Kami / Dōsojin) and with popular protectors of children; roadside stone Jizō often stand where the older phallic boundary gods stood. He is also syncretised with the Christian St. Christopher in some hidden-Christian communities, two wayfarer-saints guarding the same dangerous roads. The result is a uniquely Japanese figure: a Buddhist bodhisattva who feels, to many worshippers, like a local spirit who has simply always been there.
lore.culturalLegacy: Jizō is everywhere in Japan: thousands of stone statues line mountain paths, village boundaries, and temple precincts. The practice of mizuko kuyō — memorial rites for foetal and infant deaths — centres on him, making him a focus of modern debates about abortion, grief, and maternal responsibility. Contemporary artists and writers return to Jizō as an emblem of patient, non-judgmental compassion, and his red-bibbed image has become one of the most recognized symbols of Japanese religion worldwide.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Jizō is the Bodhisattva of refusal: he refuses to leave until everyone is safe. That sounds impossible, and it is. But the vow is not a plan; it is a posture. It says that the last and least worthy soul matters as much as the first enlightened one.

In a world that often measures worth by productivity, Jizō sits still. He does not conquer hell; he keeps it company. He does not fix grief; he clothes it in red and stays through the night. His presence beside roads and cemeteries is a reminder that the spiritual life is not an escape from suffering but a vow to remain with it.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Japanese name 地蔵 is read Jizō, from Middle Chinese 地藏 Dìzàng, which translates the Sanskrit Kṣitigarbha. 地 (ji) means 'earth' and 藏 (zō) means 'storehouse' or 'womb'. The macron on ō marks the long vowel of the Japanese reading. The full Sanskrit would require retroflex ṣ, aspirated bh, and other characters not registrable in the DNS root zone, so PUNICODEX uses the Japanese form.
lore.archaeology: Kṣitigarbha's Chinese bodhimaṇḍa is Mount Jiuhua in Anhui, where the Silla monk Jin Qiaojue (696–794) practiced and was posthumously venerated as Dizang's incarnation; the mountain's temple city and his preserved body remain a major pilgrimage destination. In Japan the documented cult begins in the Heian period — court records describe Kṣitigarbha rites performed during the Jōgan-era epidemics — while the great expansion is Kamakura: roadside stone Jizō were set up along the Tōkaidō and other travel routes as traffic, danger, and infant mortality demanded a traveler-saint. Thousands of those weathered, bibbed stones survive from that era.
